title: Krishna Defies the Conspirators
story:
Every eye in the Kuru assembly turned to Krishna, and the hall, crowded with kings, fell so quiet that the breathing of the mailed men at the door could be heard. Satyaki's warning was out. The plot of Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni, and Dussasana stood exposed — and the man they had planned to seize had heard of it, it seemed, without moving a muscle of his face. The four who had resolved on the seizure were not in the court to hear it — they had gone away from the assembly to shape their plot in secret, and their certainty would first waver only later, when Vidura brought the unwilling Duryodhana back before Krishna. What they had planned in whispers had been carried into the open by Satyaki's warning, under the eyes of the whole court.

Krishna cast his eyes on Dhritarashtra and spoke, in the midst of those who listen to others' words.

'O king,' he said, 'if these men desire to chastise me by using violence, permit them to chastise me. As for my chastising them — I dare chastise all of them together, so excited are they with rage. But I will not perpetrate any sinful and censurable act.'

He paused, and the court felt the whole meaning of what he had said settle over it: he had not asked for protection, had not called on the arrayed troops, had not even risen from his seat. Threats had been hurled across that hall for months, but no one had ever spoken like this — with the calm of a man describing the weather while holding the outcome in his hand.

'Coveting the possessions of the Pandavas, your sons will lose their own,' he went on. 'If they desire to perpetrate such a deed, Yudhishthira's object will then be easily accomplished — for, this very day, seizing these men with all that follow them, I can make them over to the sons of Pritha. What is there that is difficult of attainment by me? But I will not, in your presence, O great monarch, commit any such censurable deed as can proceed only from wrath and a sinful understanding. Let it be, O king, as this Duryodhana desires. I give permission to all your sons to do it.'

A sound went through the hall that was half wonder and half fear. The Pandavas' messenger had come to Hastinapura speaking of peace, and the court had grown used to thinking of Krishna as a negotiator — a voice, a supplicant for an agreement. But the man who sat before them now spoke as one who could end the argument between the two houses with a single motion, and who chose, instead, to withhold himself. He was not refusing the conspiracy because he feared it. He was refusing to meet it on its own ground. And in that refusal, something became clear to everyone present: the conspiracy had not failed because it had been discovered. It had failed because it was impossible, and had been impossible from the moment it was conceived.

Dhritarashtra sat blind and silent, his face turned toward the voice. Then the old king found his answer. 'Kshattri,' he said to Vidura, 'quickly bring here sinful Duryodhana, who is so covetous of sovereignty, with his friends, counsellors, brothers, and followers. I shall see if, indeed, making one more effort, I can bring him to the right path.'

So Vidura went out once more and caused the unwilling Duryodhana to enter the court, surrounded by Karna and Dussasana and the kings who followed him. The son of Dhritarashtra came back into the hall with his face set, and the kings who crowded in after him filled the aisles, so that the court, which had been hushed, grew restless again — men shifting, weapons clinking, every face turned toward the father and the son.

The defiance hung in the air of the assembly like a drawn blade. Krishna had given his permission — the calmest, most terrible permission ever spoken in that court. And Dhritarashtra, grasping at his son, was making one last attempt to keep the peace from breaking. Whether the attempt would hold, no one in that hall could say.
reflection: The striking thing about Krishna's answer is what it refuses to do: he does not rage at the plot, does not threaten the plotters, does not even protect himself. He grants them permission to try, and names his own restraint — not his power — as the only boundary he will not cross. Power held in check, he suggests, is the greater demonstration.
next_story_tease: Duryodhana's answer to that permission would draw from Krishna a sight no one in the court had ever seen.
hero_scene: Krishna, calm and unmoved in the midst of the Kuru assembly, looks directly at blind Dhritarashtra and gives his sons permission to try to seize him, while the court holds its breath.
